items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “the combined loss of water to the atmosphere by evaporation from surfaces and transpiration from plants”?
items.answer: Evapotranspiration
items.markingKey: Evapotranspiration: the combined loss of water to the atmosphere by evaporation from surfaces and transpiration from plants. [1]

items.stem: Explain how deforestation affects the hydrological cycle of a drainage basin.
items.answer: Less interception and transpiration, so less water returns to the atmosphere and local rainfall may fall; more rain reaches the ground and, with less root binding and organic matter, infiltration falls and surface runoff increases, causing faster, higher river peaks and more soil erosion.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per developed point up to [3]

items.stem: Explain why the hydrological cycle is a closed system at the global scale but an open system at the drainage-basin scale.
items.answer: Globally no water enters or leaves the Earth system, only energy; a drainage basin receives inputs of precipitation and loses outputs such as evapotranspiration and river discharge to the sea.
items.markingKey: global: no input/output of water [1]; basin: inputs and outputs [1] [2]

items.stem: Fig. 2.1 shows a systems diagram of a drainage basin, with precipitation as the input, stores (interception, surface, soil, groundwater, channel) and outputs of evapotranspiration and river discharge. Suggest why the forested basin has a higher base flow in dry weather.
items.answer: More water infiltrates and recharges soil and groundwater, which slowly feed the river between storms.
items.markingKey: infiltration / recharge [1]; slow release to river [1] [2]

items.stem: Fig. 2.1 shows a systems diagram of a drainage basin, with precipitation as the input, stores (interception, surface, soil, groundwater, channel) and outputs of evapotranspiration and river discharge. (a) Suggest one sustainable drainage (SuDS) method for the urban basin and explain how it works. (b) Explain the role of the Sun in driving the cycle.
items.answer: (a) Permeable paving, green roofs, swales or retention ponds increase infiltration or store water, slowing runoff. (b) Solar energy evaporates water and drives atmospheric circulation that moves vapour; gravity then returns water as precipitation and flow.
items.markingKey: (a) method [1]; explanation [1] [2] (b) evaporation [1]; circulation / transport [1] [2]

items.stem: Fig. 2.1 shows a systems diagram of a drainage basin, with precipitation as the input, stores (interception, surface, soil, groundwater, channel) and outputs of evapotranspiration and river discharge. (a) Name two stores and two flows in a drainage basin. (b) Explain the role of the Sun in driving the cycle.
items.answer: (a) Stores: interception, soil moisture, groundwater, surface storage, channel. Flows: infiltration, percolation, throughflow, surface runoff, groundwater flow. (b) Solar energy evaporates water and drives atmospheric circulation that moves vapour; gravity then returns water as precipitation and flow.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per two correct [2] (b) evaporation [1]; circulation / transport [1] [2]

items.stem: A student writes: “Climate change could speed up the hydrological cycle.” Is this statement correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. A warmer atmosphere increases evaporation and can hold about 7% more water vapour per °C, giving more intense rainfall and droughts.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: The volume of water stored in groundwater is about 23 514 000 km³. The flow of water out of this store by groundwater discharge is about 2 300 km³ per year. (a) Explain what is meant by residence time. (b) Explain why the residence time is only an average.
items.answer: (a) The average time a water molecule spends in a store before moving to another part of the cycle. (b) Some water passes through quickly and some stays much longer; flows vary with season and location.

items.stem: Fig. 2.1 shows a systems diagram of a drainage basin, with precipitation as the input, stores (interception, surface, soil, groundwater, channel) and outputs of evapotranspiration and river discharge. (a) Explain why river discharge rises faster after rain in the urban basin. (b) Suggest why the forested basin has a higher base flow in dry weather.
items.answer: (a) Impermeable surfaces (roads, roofs) prevent infiltration, so more surface runoff; drains carry water quickly to the river; less vegetation means little interception. (b) More water infiltrates and recharges soil and groundwater, which slowly feed the river between storms.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark per point up to [3] (b) infiltration / recharge [1]; slow release to river [1] [2]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “a continuous, directed movement of sea water driven by winds, the Earth’s rotation and differences in density”?
items.answer: Ocean current
items.markingKey: Ocean current: a continuous, directed movement of sea water driven by winds, the Earth’s rotation and differences in density. [1]

items.stem: Explain why upwelling occurs off the coast of Peru in a normal year.
items.answer: South-east trade winds blow surface water offshore and westwards (helped by the Coriolis effect); cold, nutrient-rich water rises from below to replace it.
items.markingKey: winds move surface water offshore [1]; deep cold water rises to replace it [1] [2]

items.stem: Describe the changes in the Pacific during an El Niño event.
items.answer: Trade winds weaken or reverse; warm water moves east towards South America; upwelling off Peru is suppressed; the area of rising air and rainfall shifts to the central and eastern Pacific; pressure falls in the east and rises in the west.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per change up to [3]

items.stem: Fig. 2.2 shows sea surface temperatures across the tropical Pacific in December of a normal year and of an El Niño year, with arrows showing the trade winds. Explain how the trade winds produce this pattern.
items.answer: Easterly trade winds push warm surface water westwards; this allows cold water to upwell in the east.

items.stem: A newspaper in Colombo reports that scientists have declared an El Niño event, with sea surface temperatures in the eastern Pacific 1.5 °C above average. (a) Explain how the trade winds produce this pattern. (b) Suggest how countries can prepare for El Niño events.
items.answer: (a) Easterly trade winds push warm surface water westwards; this allows cold water to upwell in the east. (b) Forecasting from ocean buoys and satellites; storing water and food; adjusting crops and fishing quotas; flood defences and emergency planning.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) 1 mark per point up to [2]

items.stem: A newspaper in Lisbon reports that scientists have declared an El Niño event, with sea surface temperatures in the eastern Pacific 1.5 °C above average. (a) Describe the normal pattern of sea surface temperature across the Pacific. (b) Suggest how countries can prepare for El Niño events.
items.answer: (a) Warm water (about 28-30 °C) builds up in the west near Indonesia and Australia; cooler water (about 20-24 °C) in the east near Peru. (b) Forecasting from ocean buoys and satellites; storing water and food; adjusting crops and fishing quotas; flood defences and emergency planning.
items.markingKey: (a) warm west [1]; cool east with data [1] [2] (b) 1 mark per point up to [2]

items.stem: A student writes: “El Niño events affect only the countries next to the Pacific Ocean.” Is this statement correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. Through teleconnections they affect weather worldwide, e.g. drought in southern Africa and India and wetter winters in the southern USA.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Table 2.2 shows the Oceanic Niño Index (3-month mean sea surface temperature anomaly, °C, in the central Pacific) from mid-1997 to early 1998: JJA +0.1, JAS +0.4, ASO +0.7, SON +1.0, OND +1.6, NDJ +2.0, DJF +1.8, JFM +1.2, FMA +0.3. An El Niño is declared when the anomaly is +0.5 °C or more for at least five consecutive overlapping periods. Determine whether these data meet the definition of an El Niño. Justify your answer.
items.answer: Yes: the anomaly is +0.5 °C or more for 6 consecutive periods (at least five).
items.markingKey: uses threshold [1]; counts consecutive periods [1] [2]

items.stem: A newspaper in Singapore reports that scientists have declared an El Niño event, with sea surface temperatures in the eastern Pacific 1.5 °C above average. (a) Explain how the trade winds produce this pattern. (b) Describe and explain the effects of El Niño on rainfall in South America and Australia.
items.answer: (a) Easterly trade winds push warm surface water westwards; this allows cold water to upwell in the east. (b) Warm water in the east causes air to rise, giving heavy rain and floods in Peru and Ecuador; sinking air over the western Pacific gives drought and bushfires in eastern Australia.
items.markingKey: (a) [2] (b) 1 mark each region with explanation up to [4]

items.stem: Which term matches this definition: “the enrichment of water with nutrients such as nitrates and phosphates, causing algal blooms and oxygen depletion”?
items.answer: Eutrophication
items.markingKey: Eutrophication: the enrichment of water with nutrients such as nitrates and phosphates, causing algal blooms and oxygen depletion. [1]

items.stem: Describe the stages of eutrophication.
items.answer: Nutrients (nitrates, phosphates) enter water; algae grow rapidly forming a bloom; light is blocked so plants below die; algae and plants die and are decomposed by bacteria; bacteria use up dissolved oxygen; fish and other animals die.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per stage in sequence up to [4]

items.stem: Explain why over-abstraction of groundwater is a problem in coastal areas.
items.answer: The water table falls and the pressure of fresh water drops, so salt water from the sea moves into the aquifer (saltwater intrusion), making wells unusable; land may also subside.
items.markingKey: falling water table [1]; saltwater intrusion [1]; consequence [1] [3]

items.stem: Name one example of a polluted freshwater body you have studied and, for that example, explain the causes of the pollution.
items.answer: the Ganges (Ganga), India: About 3 billion litres per day of mostly untreated sewage from over 100 cities; industrial waste from tanneries in Kanpur (chromium); agricultural runoff; religious offerings and cremation remains.
items.markingKey: 1 mark named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. sources (point and diffuse), named pollutants, effects [4]

items.stem: Students measured water quality on River Densu in Ghana at site A (500 m upstream of a food-processing factory), site B (50 m downstream) and site C (2 km downstream). Dissolved oxygen (mg/l): A 9.3, B 4.0, C 7.6. BOD (mg/l): A 2.7, B 11.3, C 4.9. (a) Calculate the percentage decrease in dissolved oxygen between site A and site B. (b) Describe the changes in BOD downstream.
items.answer: (a) 57.0% (b) BOD rises sharply from 2.7 mg/l at A to 11.3 mg/l at B, then falls to 4.9 mg/l at C but stays above the upstream value.

items.stem: For Lake Erie, USA and Canada or another example of a polluted freshwater body, briefly evaluate the strategies used to improve water quality.
items.answer: Lake Erie, USA and Canada: The 1972 Great Lakes Water Quality Agreement limited phosphates in detergents and upgraded sewage works, so the lake recovered by the 1980s; current targets aim to cut phosphorus loads by 40% from farms.
items.markingKey: 1 mark named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. named strategies with outcomes; limitations; judgement [4]

items.stem: Explain how persistent pollutants such as mercury can harm top predators.
items.answer: Mercury is not broken down and is stored in tissues (bioaccumulation); at each trophic level organisms eat many prey, so concentration increases (biomagnification); top predators and humans receive toxic doses (e.g. Minamata, Japan).
items.markingKey: bioaccumulation [1]; biomagnification [1]; effect / example [1] [3]

items.stem: Explain how physical factors in a drainage basin can increase flood risk.
items.answer: Intense or prolonged rainfall; saturated or frozen ground; steep slopes; impermeable rock or clay soils; small, circular basins with a high drainage density; snowmelt.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per factor with explanation up to [3]

items.stem: Explain how human activities can increase the risk of flooding.
items.answer: Urbanisation (impermeable surfaces, drains); deforestation (less interception, more runoff); building on floodplains; channel straightening that speeds water downstream; farming that compacts soil.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per developed point up to [3]

items.stem: A town near Dhaka built on a floodplain has flooded three times in ten years. The council is considering levees, a flood-relief channel or upstream tree planting. Explain why the urban basin has a higher and earlier peak.
items.answer: Impermeable surfaces and drains send rainwater quickly to the river with little infiltration or interception.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point up to [2]

items.stem: A town near Dhaka built on a floodplain has flooded three times in ten years. The council is considering levees, a flood-relief channel or upstream tree planting. (a) Calculate the difference in lag time between the two basins. (b) Explain the purpose of land-use zoning on floodplains.
items.answer: (a) 12 hours (18 − 6) (b) It restricts building in high-risk areas, so fewer people and property are exposed, and keeps the floodplain free to store water.

items.stem: A town near Manila built on a floodplain has flooded three times in ten years. The council is considering levees, a flood-relief channel or upstream tree planting. (a) Explain why the urban basin has a higher and earlier peak. (b) Explain the purpose of land-use zoning on floodplains.
items.answer: (a) Impermeable surfaces and drains send rainwater quickly to the river with little infiltration or interception. (b) It restricts building in high-risk areas, so fewer people and property are exposed, and keeps the floodplain free to store water.

items.stem: Explain why droughts may become more frequent with climate change.
items.answer: Higher temperatures increase evaporation; rainfall patterns shift with more variable and less reliable rain in some regions; earlier snowmelt reduces summer flows.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per point up to [3]

items.stem: For the 2019 Chennai water crisis, India or another example of a flood or drought event, briefly describe the impacts on people and the environment.
items.answer: the 2019 Chennai water crisis, India: Piped supply cut; residents queued for tankers; offices and restaurants closed; water prices rose sharply, hitting the poor hardest.
items.markingKey: 1 mark named, located example; up to 3 marks for accurate, place-specific points. social, economic and environmental impacts with figures [4]

items.stem: A town near Kuala Lumpur built on a floodplain has flooded three times in ten years. The council is considering levees, a flood-relief channel or upstream tree planting. (a) Calculate the difference in lag time between the two basins. (b) Compare hard and soft engineering approaches to reducing the flood risk.
items.answer: (a) 12 hours (18 − 6) (b) Hard (levees, channels, dams) give immediate high protection but are costly, may move the problem downstream and look unnatural; soft (afforestation, wetlands, zoning) are cheaper, sustainable and support wildlife but take time and may protect less in extreme floods.

items.stem: Describe the processes by which water moves from the ocean to a river.
items.answer: Evaporation from the ocean; condensation to form clouds; transport by wind; precipitation over land; then infiltration, throughflow, groundwater flow or surface runoff into the river.

items.stem: Explain the impacts of El Niño on the Peruvian fishing industry.
items.answer: Warm water suppresses upwelling so nutrient supply falls; plankton decline; anchoveta stocks fall or move, so catches collapse (e.g. 1972-73 and 1997-98), causing job losses and less fishmeal for export.
items.markingKey: less upwelling / nutrients [1]; food chain effect [1]; economic impact [1] [3]

items.stem: To what extent is it true that the impacts of El Niño are mainly negative?
items.answer: For: El Niño causes floods in Peru and Ecuador, drought and fires in Indonesia and Australia, fishery collapse off Peru, and coral bleaching; the 1997-98 event caused about US$35 billion of damage. Against: Some areas benefit: fewer Atlantic hurricanes, milder winters in North America, more rain for some dry regions and growth of shrimp catches in Ecuador. Judgement: The impacts are mostly negative, especially for vulnerable economies, but they vary between regions and some places benefit.

items.stem: A student writes: “Groundwater is always safe to drink because it is filtered by rocks.” Is this statement correct? Explain your answer.

items.stem: Explain why groundwater is an important source of water in many countries.
items.answer: It is available all year, even in droughts; it is usually naturally filtered and cleaner than surface water; it is widely distributed and can be reached by wells close to users.

items.stem: Recharge of an aquifer in Punjab, India is about 0.4 km³ per year, but abstraction for irrigation and towns is 1.3 km³ per year. About 20 km³ of usable water remains in storage. Suggest two strategies to manage the aquifer more sustainably.
items.answer: Drip irrigation; growing less water-intensive crops; metering and pricing water; licensing wells; artificial recharge using stored storm water or treated wastewater.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per strategy up to [2]

items.stem: Evaluate the view that pollution is a greater threat to fresh water supply than over-abstraction. In your answer you should consider: sewage; agriculture.
items.answer: For: Untreated sewage, industrial waste and fertiliser runoff make water unsafe (e.g. the Ganges, Lake Erie); about 2 billion people use a drinking water source contaminated with faeces. Against: Over-abstraction empties aquifers and rivers (e.g. the Ogallala aquifer, the Aral Sea, Chennai in 2019) and causes saltwater intrusion and subsidence, permanently reducing supply. Judgement: Both are serious; pollution can often be treated, while over-abstraction of fossil groundwater may be irreversible.

items.stem: Explain how ocean currents redistribute heat around the Earth.
items.answer: Warm surface currents carry heat from the tropics towards the poles (e.g. Gulf Stream), and cold currents return cooler water towards the equator, reducing the temperature difference between latitudes.
items.markingKey: warm currents poleward [1]; cold currents equatorward [1]; effect on climate [1] [3]

items.stem: Table 2.2 shows the Oceanic Niño Index (3-month mean sea surface temperature anomaly, °C, in the central Pacific) from mid-1982 to early 1983: JJA +0.1, JAS +0.4, ASO +0.7, SON +1.0, OND +1.0, NDJ +1.2, DJF +1.1, JFM +0.7, FMA +0.3. An El Niño is declared when the anomaly is +0.5 °C or more for at least five consecutive overlapping periods. (a) Calculate the mean anomaly over the nine periods. (b) Classify the strength of the event (weak 0.5-0.9, moderate 1.0-1.4, strong 1.5-1.9, very strong ≥ 2.0 °C peak).
items.answer: (a) +0.72 °C (b) Moderate

items.stem: Table 2.2 shows the Oceanic Niño Index (3-month mean sea surface temperature anomaly, °C, in the central Pacific) from mid-1997 to early 1998: JJA +0.1, JAS +0.4, ASO +0.7, SON +1.0, OND +1.0, NDJ +1.2, DJF +1.1, JFM +0.7, FMA +0.3. An El Niño is declared when the anomaly is +0.5 °C or more for at least five consecutive overlapping periods. (a) State the period with the highest anomaly and its value. (b) Suggest the likely impact of this event on the anchoveta catch off Peru, giving a reason.
items.answer: (a) NDJ: +1.2 °C (b) The catch would fall because warmer water suppresses upwelling, so fewer nutrients and less plankton support fewer fish.
items.markingKey: (a) [1] (b) catch falls [1]; reason [1] [2]

items.stem: “The impacts of El Niño are mainly negative.” To what extent do you agree with this statement? Refer to examples you have studied. In your answer you should consider: teleconnections; droughts and floods; fisheries.
items.answer: For: El Niño causes floods in Peru and Ecuador, drought and fires in Indonesia and Australia, fishery collapse off Peru, and coral bleaching; the 1997-98 event caused about US$35 billion of damage. Against: Some areas benefit: fewer Atlantic hurricanes, milder winters in North America, more rain for some dry regions and growth of shrimp catches in Ecuador. Judgement: The impacts are mostly negative, especially for vulnerable economies, but they vary between regions and some places benefit.

items.stem: What is meant by the term “biochemical oxygen demand (BOD)”?
options: An aquifer sandwiched between impermeable rock layers, so water is under pressure.
Pollution entering water from a single identifiable source, such as a sewage outfall or factory pipe.
The amount of dissolved oxygen used by microorganisms to break down organic matter in a water sample.
Pollution entering water from many scattered sources, such as fertiliser runoff from farmland.
items.answer: The amount of dissolved oxygen used by microorganisms to break down organic matter in a water sample.
items.markingKey: Biochemical oxygen demand (BOD): the amount of dissolved oxygen used by microorganisms to break down organic matter in a water sample. [1]

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Diffuse pollution is harder to control than point source pollution.” Is this statement correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. It comes from many scattered sources, so it is difficult to identify and regulate each one.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Describe how sewage is treated before discharge into a river.
items.answer: Screening removes large objects; primary sedimentation removes solids; secondary (biological) treatment uses bacteria in aeration tanks or trickling filters to break down organic matter; tertiary treatment may remove nutrients or disinfect.
items.markingKey: 1 mark per stage up to [3]

items.stem: Students measured water quality on River Tees at site A (500 m upstream of a dairy farm), site B (50 m downstream) and site C (2 km downstream). Dissolved oxygen (mg/l): A 9.2, B 4.5, C 8.2. BOD (mg/l): A 1.7, B 15.0, C 5.5. Explain the relationship between BOD and dissolved oxygen at site B.
items.answer: Organic waste from the discharge is decomposed by aerobic bacteria; high BOD means the bacteria use up dissolved oxygen, so oxygen falls.
items.markingKey: organic matter decomposed [1]; bacteria use oxygen [1] [2]

items.stem: Recharge of the aquifer under the North China Plain is about 1 km³ per year, but abstraction for irrigation and towns is 2.8 km³ per year. About 150 km³ of usable water remains in storage. Water-saving irrigation reduces abstraction by 50%. Calculate the new lifetime of the aquifer, or state whether it would become sustainable.
items.answer: New abstraction 1.40 km³; deficit 0.400 km³; lifetime 375 years.
items.markingKey: new abstraction 1.40 [1]; comparison / new lifetime [1] [2]

items.stem: “Pollution is a greater threat to fresh water supply than over-abstraction.” Discuss.
items.answer: For: Untreated sewage, industrial waste and fertiliser runoff make water unsafe (e.g. the Ganges, Lake Erie); about 2 billion people use a drinking water source contaminated with faeces. Against: Over-abstraction empties aquifers and rivers (e.g. the Ogallala aquifer, the Aral Sea, Chennai in 2019) and causes saltwater intrusion and subsidence, permanently reducing supply. Judgement: Both are serious; pollution can often be treated, while over-abstraction of fossil groundwater may be irreversible.

items.stem: In a class discussion, a student says: “Floods can bring benefits to farmers.” Is this statement correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Correct. They deposit fertile silt and recharge soil water, e.g. on the floodplains of Bangladesh.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: A news article states: “Drought is only caused by a lack of rainfall.” Is this statement correct? Explain your answer.
items.answer: Not correct. High temperatures, evaporation and human over-use of water also cause water shortages.
items.markingKey: 1 mark correct judgement; 1 mark accurate explanation [2]

items.stem: Annual maximum discharges were recorded for the Rhine at Cologne over 50 years and ranked (1 = largest). Recurrence interval RI = (n + 1) ÷ m, where n is the number of years and m the rank. rank 1: 1 363 cumecs; rank 4: 1 250 cumecs; rank 5: 1 004 cumecs; rank 7: 754 cumecs. (a) Calculate the recurrence interval of the flood of 1 250 cumecs. (b) Calculate the probability that a flood at least as large as 1 250 cumecs occurs in any one year. (c) Explain why recurrence intervals should be used with caution when planning flood defences.
items.answer: (a) 12.8 years (b) 0.0784 (7.84%) (c) The record may be short; climate change and land-use change alter flood frequency; a 1-in-100-year flood can occur in consecutive years.

items.stem: Fig. 2.4 shows flood hydrographs for two drainage basins after the same storm. Basin X (urban) peaks at 85 cumecs 6 hours after peak rainfall; basin Y (forested) peaks at 30 cumecs 18 hours after peak rainfall. (a) Compare hard and soft engineering approaches to reducing the flood risk. (b) Explain the purpose of land-use zoning on floodplains.
items.answer: (a) Hard (levees, channels, dams) give immediate high protection but are costly, may move the problem downstream and look unnatural; soft (afforestation, wetlands, zoning) are cheaper, sustainable and support wildlife but take time and may protect less in extreme floods. (b) It restricts building in high-risk areas, so fewer people and property are exposed, and keeps the floodplain free to store water.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark each comparative point up to [4] (b) [2]
